b OurBigBook.com
The given complex numbers have positive real parts, so argz1​=arctanA and argz2​=arctanB. Their product is
z1​z2​=(1−AB)+i(A+B).
(21)
By the assumed complex argument ranges, this product also has positive real part, hence 1−AB>0. Its complex argument is consequently arctan[(A+B)/(1−AB)], with no extra multiple of π. Since multiplication adds complex arguments,
arctanA+arctanB=arctan(1−ABA+B​).​
(22)
This proves the arctangent addition formula under the stated branch restriction. For arbitrary real A,B, the principal inverse tangent formula can require adding or subtracting π when AB>1.

Thus Q is invariant under the common rotation.

From the same multiplication, the imaginary part is

Its magnitude is the area of their parallelogram; its sign is positive when the oriented angle from v2​ to v1​ has positive sine. e OurBigBook.com
Since x=cosy with real y, necessarily −1≤x≤1. Use Euler's formula and set w=eiy=0. Then
2x=w+w−1,w2−2xw+1=0,
(27)
so the quadratic equation gives w=x±i1−x2​. Let q=x+i1−x2​. It lies on the upper half of the unit circle, so q=eiθ with 0≤θ≤π. Choose the complex logarithm value lnq=iθ, taking ln(−1)=iπ at x=−1. The two roots are e±iθ, so eiy=e±iθ gives y=±θ+2nπ.
Because ilnq=−θ, this set of real solutions is exactly
y=±iln(x+i1−x2​)+2nπ,n∈Z.​
(28)
The formula includes x=±1: the two sign families then coincide after adjusting n. No real y exists if ∣x∣>1.

∑n=0N−1​einθ=1−eiθ1−eiNθ​=ei(N−1)θ/2sin(θ/2)sin(Nθ/2)​.

The second equality follows by factoring 1−eit=−2ieit/2sin(t/2) in numerator and denominator. Taking real parts proves the finite trigonometric sum identity

Take the dumbbell axis to be the z axis, with its midpoint at z=0. The right-hand sphere has centre z=αa and radius R=βa, while its junction with the cylinder is at z=γa. Put d=(α−γ)a, so 0<d<R. The Pythagorean theorem in a meridional cross-section gives the handle radius H from H2+d2=R2. Thus
H=aβ2−(α−γ)2​.​
(31)

b

Solution

b OurBigBook.com
Use cylindrical coordinates (r,ϕ,z) about the dumbbell axis. Their Jacobian determinant contributes the volume factor r, so the handle's mass is the volume integral
Mh​=ρ∫−γaγa​∫02π​∫0H​rdrdϕdz=ρ(2γa)(2π)2H2​.
(32)
Inserting the radius from part (a) yields
Mh​=2πργa3[β2−(α−γ)2].​
(33)

c

Words: 95 Articles: 1
12 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 95
c OurBigBook.com
Centre cylindrical coordinates on the right-hand sphere, with the axial coordinate s=z−αa positive outwards. Using R=βa and d=(α−γ)a, the retained solid satisfies
−d≤s≤R,0≤r≤R2−s2​,0≤ϕ<2π.
(34)
In particular, it contains more than a hemisphere; it is the small cap on the inward side that has been removed. The volume integral for its mass, including the Jacobian determinant r, is
Me​​=ρ∫−dR​∫02π​∫0R2−s2​​rdrdϕds=πρ∫−dR​(R2−s2)ds=πρ(32R3​+R2d−3d3​).​
(35)
Thus each end piece has mass
Me​=πρa3[32β3​+β2(α−γ)−3(α−γ)3​].​
(36)
Equivalently this is the volume of a spherical cap with height R+d, multiplied by the uniform mass density.

d OurBigBook.com
Use spherical coordinates (r,θ,ϕ) centred on the right-hand sphere, with polar axis pointing outwards along s. The Jacobian determinant is r2sinθ, and the retained region is r≤R with rcosθ≥−d.
For 0≤r≤d, every polar angle 0≤θ≤π is allowed. For d<r≤R, the cut requires 0≤θ≤arccos(−d/r). Splitting the volume integral at r=d therefore gives
Me​====​ρ∫02π​[∫0d​∫0π​r2sinθdθdr+∫dR​∫0arccos(−d/r)​r2sinθdθdr]dϕ2πρ[2∫0d​r2dr+∫dR​r2(1+rd​)dr]2πρ[32d3​+3R3−d3​+2d​(R2−d2)]πρ(32R3​+R2d−3d3​).​​
(37)
Substitution of R=βa and d=(α−γ)a reproduces the mass in part (c). The radial split avoids integrating over a polar angle range independent of r, which would incorrectly include part of the removed spherical cap.

Equivalently, since γ+δ=α,

The zero solution satisfies both the ordinary differential equation and the initial condition. Let P=μ(x)(xy−16x−x3) and Q=μ(x)(16+x2). An exact differential form must satisfy Py​=Qx​. These partial derivatives give
xμ=(16+x2)μ′+2xμ,μμ′​=−16+x2x​.

Taking antiderivatives produces ln∣μ∣=−21​ln(16+x2)+C. A convenient nonzero integrating factor for a differential one-form is therefore
μ(x)=16+x2​1​.​
(46)
An explicit potential, which also proves global exactness, is
F(x,y)=y16+x2​−31​(16+x2)3/2.

1−αzx​=−βqzx​,−αzy​=q(1−βzy​).

Consequently

The scaling relation says that z is a homogeneous function of degree n. Fix (x,y) and differentiate the identity with respect to the positive parameter λ. The chain rule gives
xzx​(λx,λy)+yzy​(λx,λy)=nλn−1z(x,y).
(55)
Setting λ=1 proves the Euler theorem for homogeneous functions identity
xzx​+yzy​=nz.​
(56)
Differentiate once more with respect to λ, using equality of the mixed partial derivatives for the assumed twice continuously differentiable function:
x2zxx​(λx,λy)+2xyzxy​(λx,λy)+y2zyy​(λx,λy)=n(n−1)λn−2z(x,y).
(57)
At λ=1 this is the second-order Euler identity for homogeneous functions:
x2zxx​+2xyzxy​+y2zyy​=n(n−1)z.​
(58)
The repeated parameter differentiation accounts for the factor n(n−1), rather than n2.

Taylor's theorem gives a finite Taylor polynomial of degree n, consisting of the first n+1 terms, and a remainder:
f(x)=j=0∑n​j!f(j)(a)​(x−a)j+Rn+1​(x).​
(59)
In the Taylor theorem with Lagrange remainder form, assuming the required derivatives exist on an interval containing a and x,
Rn+1​(x)=(n+1)!f(n+1)(ξ)​(x−a)n+1,​
(60)
for some ξ strictly between a and x when x=a; at x=a the remainder is zero. In particular, if ∣f(n+1)∣≤M on that segment, then ∣Rn+1​(x)∣≤M∣x−a∣n+1/(n+1)!. This is a finite expansion; it does not assume equality with an infinite Taylor series.

For necessity, take the positive sequence xn​=1/(2πn)→0. Then cos(1/xn​)=1, so f(xn​)=(2πn)−p. For p=0 this equals 1; for p<0 it tends to +∞. In neither case does it tend to f(0)=0, so continuity fails. Consequently
